questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: build a unit vector from the components of a given vector
questions.stem: A vector in the plane has components ⟨6, −8⟩. How is the unit vector pointing along that same direction built?

options.text: Divide each component by the magnitude, which leaves 0.6 and −0.8
Divide the magnitude by each component in turn, which reverses the ratios
options.misconception: believes a unit vector comes from dividing the magnitude by the components

options.text: Rescale only the component of larger size so that it equals one exactly
options.misconception: believes normalising means forcing the biggest component to equal one

options.text: Subtract each component from the magnitude to strip away the length
options.misconception: believes removing the length means subtracting it from each component

questions.explanation: A unit vector has magnitude one and the same direction, so dividing every component by the magnitude rescales length without turning anything. Here the magnitude is √(36 + 64) = 10, and 6 over 10 and −8 over 10 give 0.6 and −0.8, whose squares sum to one. Normalising only the larger component would give a vector of magnitude √2 rather than one, and subtracting the magnitude would not preserve direction at all.
questions.hint: Ask what operation leaves the direction alone while forcing the length to equal one.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: compute the magnitude of a vector from its components
questions.stem: A displacement in the plane has components ⟨3, −4⟩. What is the magnitude of that displacement? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squared components, so √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. Adding the components instead would give −1, which is only the signed horizontal part, and taking the square root of the sum without squaring first would give √7. The result is the ordinary three-four-five right triangle, whose hypotenuse is 5.
questions.hint: Square each component, add, then take the square root.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: interpret a position vector as the displacement from the origin to a point
questions.stem: A point P of the plane has coordinates (4, −1). What does the position vector of P record?

options.text: The displacement from the origin to P, namely the arrow ⟨4, −1⟩
The displacement from P back to the origin, namely the arrow ⟨−4, 1⟩
options.misconception: believes a position vector points from the point toward the origin

options.text: The shortest distance from P to the origin, which is a number not an arrow
options.misconception: believes a position vector is only the numerical length from the origin

options.text: The direction from P toward the nearest coordinate axis, with no origin
options.misconception: believes a position vector is measured from an axis rather than the origin

questions.explanation: The position vector of a point is the unique vector that carries the origin to that point, so it has exactly the point's coordinates as its components. Its length happens to be the distance from the origin, but a vector carries direction as well, and the vector from P back to the origin is the negative of the position vector, not the position vector itself.
questions.hint: Ask which arrow, when drawn, actually arrives at the given point.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: compute one component of a unit vector from the components of a vector
questions.stem: A vector has components ⟨6, 8⟩. What is the first component of the unit vector that points along the same direction? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The magnitude is √(36 + 64) = 10, and dividing the first component by that magnitude gives 6 over 10 = 0.6. Leaving the component undivided would give 6, and dividing by the sum of the components, 14, would give a different wrong value. As a check, 0.6 squared plus 0.8 squared is 0.36 plus 0.64, which is exactly 1.
questions.hint: Compute the magnitude first, then divide the component by it.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: use a vanishing dot product as the test for perpendicular vectors
questions.stem: Two nonzero vectors u and v are given. What does the statement u · v = 0 tell you about them?

options.text: The two vectors meet at a right angle, because the dot product is |u||v|cos θ
The two vectors have equal magnitude, since a zero sum cancels equal parts
options.misconception: believes a zero dot product means the two magnitudes are equal

options.text: The two vectors are opposites, so one equals the negative of the other
options.misconception: believes a zero dot product means the vectors are negatives of each other

options.text: The two vectors are parallel, which is the only way a product can vanish
options.misconception: believes a vanishing product forces the vectors to be parallel

questions.explanation: The dot product equals the product of the magnitudes times the cosine of the angle between them, so for nonzero vectors it is zero exactly when the cosine is zero, that is when the angle is a right angle. Opposite vectors have cosine −1 and a negative dot product, and parallel vectors have cosine one and a positive dot product, so neither of those can produce a zero.
questions.hint: Recall the geometric meaning of the product formula before deciding.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: add two vectors by components and take the magnitude of the result
questions.stem: Two displacements are ⟨3, −2⟩ and ⟨−1, 5⟩. What is the magnitude of their sum? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Adding componentwise gives ⟨2, 3⟩, and the magnitude of that is √(4 + 9) = √13, which is about 3.6056. Adding the magnitudes instead would give 3.606 as well only by coincidence, but adding the raw components gives 5 and would describe something else entirely. The addition must happen in components before any length is taken.
questions.hint: Add the two components separately, then apply the magnitude formula once.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: describe the combined effect of multiplying a vector by a scalar
questions.stem: A nonzero vector v is multiplied by the scalar −2. What happens to the vector?

options.text: It keeps its line through the origin but points the opposite way and is twice as long
It keeps its direction and becomes half as long, since the sign is ignored
options.misconception: believes a negative scalar only shortens a vector without reversing it

options.text: It keeps its length and turns through a right angle, since the sign rotates it
options.misconception: believes a negative scalar rotates a vector by ninety degrees

options.text: It is unchanged in length but its direction is reflected in the x-axis
options.misconception: believes a negative scalar reflects a vector rather than reversing it

questions.explanation: A positive scalar stretches or shrinks along the existing direction, and a negative scalar additionally reverses that direction, so −2 doubles the length and sends the arrow to the opposite side of the origin. Reflection in an axis is a different operation that needs a matrix, and a scalar never turns a vector through a right angle.
questions.hint: Separate the magnitude of the scalar from its sign.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: find the magnitude of a scalar multiple of a vector
questions.stem: The vector ⟨3, 4⟩ is multiplied by the scalar −2. What is the magnitude of the resulting vector? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The original magnitude is √(9 + 16) = 5, and taking the magnitude after scaling by −2 multiplies that by 2, giving 10. Computing the scaled components first gives ⟨−6, −8⟩, whose magnitude is √(36 + 64) = 10, confirming the rule. A negative scalar changes direction but cannot change length beyond the size of the scalar itself.
questions.hint: Recall how the magnitude of a scalar multiple relates to the original magnitude.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Angle revealed by a dot product
questions.learningObjective: explain how a dot product determines the angle between two vectors
questions.stem: Two vectors u and v have positive magnitudes. How does the sign of their dot product tell you about the angle between them?

options.text: A positive product means an acute angle, a negative product an obtuse one, and zero a right one
A positive product means the vectors are perpendicular, since products cancel at right angles
options.misconception: believes a positive product signals a right angle instead of an acute one

options.text: The sign of the product gives no information, only the magnitude of the product matters
options.misconception: believes the sign of a dot product carries no angular information

options.text: A positive product means the vectors point in the same direction along one line
options.misconception: believes a positive dot product can only mean parallel vectors

questions.explanation: Dividing the dot product by the product of the magnitudes gives the cosine of the angle, and the cosine is positive on the first quadrant, negative on the second, and zero at a right angle. The magnitude of the product only says how much of the maximum possible product occurs, while the sign says which side of a right angle the vectors sit on.
questions.hint: Divide the product by the magnitudes and think about the cosine.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: compute a dot product from given components
questions.stem: Compute the dot product of the vectors ⟨2, 3⟩ and ⟨−1, 4⟩. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Multiply matching components and add: 2 times −1 plus 3 times 4, which is −2 + 12 = 10. Adding the corresponding components instead would give ⟨1, 7⟩, which is a vector and not the product at all. As a check, the result is positive, so the angle is acute, and indeed the cosine of that angle works out to 10 over √13 times √17.
questions.hint: Multiply the first components together, then the second components, then add.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: write a parametric equation for a line from a point and a direction
questions.stem: A particle passes through the point (2, 3) with direction of travel ⟨4, −1⟩. Which pair of equations parametrises that line?

options.text: x equals 2 plus 4t and y equals 3 minus t, so the given point sits at t = 0
x equals 2t plus 4 and y equals 3t minus 1, making the point a coefficient of t
options.misconception: believes a point can be introduced by multiplying the parameter by it

options.text: x equals 4t plus 2 and y equals minus t plus 3, which flips the direction vector
options.misconception: believes reordering the direction components describes the same line

options.text: x equals 2 plus t and y equals 3 minus 4t, which shrinks both direction components
options.misconception: believes the direction components may be rescaled to one and a half

questions.explanation: A parametric line is the point plus a multiple of the direction, so x equals 2 plus 4t and y equals 3 minus t. At t = 0 the point is exactly (2, 3), and moving t by one shifts by the whole direction ⟨4, −1⟩. Reversing the direction would trace the same set of points but in the opposite order, so option C is the same line, though not the stated travel.
questions.hint: Check which expression gives the stated point when the parameter is zero.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: find the angle between two vectors from their dot product and magnitudes
questions.stem: Find the angle in degrees between the vectors ⟨3, 0⟩ and ⟨1, 1⟩, taking the smaller angle. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The magnitudes are 3 and √2, and the dot product is 3, so the cosine is 3 divided by 3√2, which is 1 over √2, and the angle is 45 degrees. As an independent check, the vector ⟨1, 1⟩ makes an angle of 45 degrees with the positive x-axis by the tangent of one, and ⟨3, 0⟩ lies along that axis, so the angle between them is 45 degrees.
questions.hint: Divide the dot product by the product of the magnitudes, then invert the cosine.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: convert a point with a zero coordinate into a polar pair
questions.stem: A point sits at the Cartesian coordinates (0, 6). First report its radius r, then report its angle θ in degrees measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis.

options.text: r is 6 and θ is 90, putting the point on the positive y-axis
r is 6 and θ is 0, putting the point along the positive x-axis
options.misconception: believes the first coordinate of the pair is always the angle

options.text: r is 0 and θ is 6, reading the Cartesian pair as a polar pair directly
options.misconception: believes the coordinate pair can be reused unchanged as a polar pair

options.text: r is 6 and θ is 270, taking the long way round to reach the point
options.misconception: believes an angle must exceed 180 degrees for a point on the y-axis

questions.explanation: The radius is the distance from the origin, √(0 + 36) = 6, and the angle follows from the location: a point straight up the positive y-axis has angle 90 degrees. Reading the pair as (r, θ) without transforming would be a category error, since the two coordinate systems order the information differently, and 270 degrees also reaches the same point but sweeps through the lower half first.
questions.hint: Compute the distance from the origin, then name the axis the point sits on.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: interpret a vector projection as the shadow of one vector along another
questions.stem: You project vector v onto a nonzero vector u. How is the resulting vector built?

options.text: Scale u by the factor (u · v) divided by the squared magnitude of u
Scale v by the factor (u · v) divided by the squared magnitude of v
options.misconception: believes the scale factor is built from the magnitude of the vector being projected

options.text: Scale u by the factor (u · v) divided by the magnitude of u alone
options.misconception: believes the denominator in the projection factor is the magnitude, not its square

options.text: Scale the sum u plus v by the factor (u · v) divided by the squared magnitude of u
options.misconception: believes the projection must add the two vectors before scaling

questions.explanation: The projection of v onto u is the component of v that lies along u, and it is obtained by scaling u by the dimensionless factor (u · v) over (u · u), which is the squared magnitude of u. That factor is the cosine of the angle times the length of v, so the projection lands on the line through u at the right distance. Using the magnitude instead of its square would miss the final division by the length of u.
questions.hint: The scale factor must be dimensionless, so check the units of the denominator.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: solve for the unknown component that makes two vectors perpendicular
questions.stem: Find the value of k that makes the vectors ⟨k, 2⟩ and ⟨3, −1⟩ perpendicular to each other. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Perpendicularity means a zero dot product, so 3k plus 2 times −1 equals zero, that is 3k = 2 and k = 2 over 3. Multiplying the components instead would give 3k − 2 = 0 as well by accident of signs, but substituting back confirms 3 times 2 over 3 minus 2 is exactly zero, and the vectors are nonzero, so the right angle is genuine.
questions.hint: Set the dot product equal to zero and solve the resulting linear equation.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: write a parametric equation for a circle with a stated direction of travel
questions.stem: A circle of radius 5 is centred at the origin and is to be traced once counterclockwise starting from the point (5, 0). Which parametrisation does that?

options.text: x equals 5 cos t and y equals 5 sin t, with t running over 0 to 2π
x equals 5 sin t and y equals 5 cos t, with t running over 0 to 2π
options.misconception: believes swapping sine and cosine still traces the circle counterclockwise

options.text: x equals 5 cos t and y equals minus 5 sin t, with t running over 0 to 2π
options.misconception: believes a sign change on one component keeps the direction of travel

options.text: x equals 5t and y equals 5t, with t running over 0 to 2π
options.misconception: believes multiplying the radius by the parameter traces a circle

questions.explanation: Both sine and cosine of the same angle are needed so that x squared plus y squared stays at 25 for every value of the parameter. The starting point fixes the phase: at t = 0 the point must be (5, 0), which only the cosine form gives, and the second component must increase near t = 0 to move upward, which is the unnegated sine. Swapping the two components starts at (0, 5) instead.
questions.hint: Test each pair at the parameter value where the path must start.

questions.learningObjective: compute a component of a vector projection
questions.stem: Project the vector ⟨5, 3⟩ onto the vector ⟨2, 1⟩. What is the first component of the resulting projection vector? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The dot product of the two vectors is 10 + 3 = 13 and the squared magnitude of ⟨2, 1⟩ is 5, so the scale factor is 13 over 5. Multiplying the first component of ⟨2, 1⟩ gives 26 over 5, which is 5.2. The check is that the leftover ⟨5 − 5.2, 3 − 2.6⟩ is orthogonal to ⟨2, 1⟩, and its dot product with that vector is indeed zero.

questions.learningObjective: locate horizontal and vertical tangents of a parametrised curve from its rate of change
questions.stem: A curve is given parametrically by x of t and y of t. Which rates at a point decide whether the curve has a horizontal or a vertical tangent there?

options.text: The horizontal case has dy over dt zero with dx over dt nonzero, the reverse giving vertical
Both tangents need dy over dt zero, and the tangent is horizontal when dx over dt is larger
options.misconception: believes a zero dy rate alone decides between horizontal and vertical tangents

options.text: The horizontal case has dx over dt zero, and the vertical case has dx over dt equal to one
options.misconception: believes a unit value of dx rate marks a vertical tangent

options.text: Neither rate matters, because the tangent is found from the second derivatives only
options.misconception: believes tangent direction must be read from second derivatives

questions.explanation: The tangent direction is the velocity vector ⟨dx over dt, dy over dt⟩, and a horizontal tangent points along the x-axis exactly when the vertical component vanishes while the horizontal one does not, otherwise the point is a genuine stop. A vertical tangent is the same statement with the roles exchanged, and using second derivatives would describe curvature rather than direction.
questions.hint: Look at which component of the rate vector vanishes, and check the other is not zero too.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the slope of a parametrised curve at a given parameter value
questions.stem: A curve is given by x of t equal to t squared plus 1 and y of t equal to 3t. What is the slope of the curve at t equal to 2? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The slope is the rate of change of y with respect to x, so it is the ratio of the two rates: 3 over 2t, and at t = 2 that is 3 over 4, which is 0.75. Dividing the rates the other way round would give 4 over 3, the reciprocal, and confirming with a small finite step of 0.000001 in t reproduces 0.75 to five decimals.
questions.hint: Differentiate both coordinates, then divide the y rate by the x rate.

questions.learningObjective: distinguish speed from velocity for a moving particle

The speed is −5, because the negative first component makes the whole value negative
options.misconception: believes a negative velocity component makes the speed a negative number

options.text: The speed is 1, because the ratio of the components is the meaningful rate of travel
options.misconception: believes a ratio of velocity components measures how fast something moves

options.text: The speed is 7, because the magnitudes of the components are what must be added
options.misconception: believes a speed comes from adding the absolute values of the components

questions.explanation: Speed is the length of the velocity arrow, √(9 + 16) = 5, and a length cannot come out negative, so the sign of a velocity component says which way the particle moves, not how fast. Adding the component magnitudes would give 7, which is the taxicab distance, and the ratio of components describes direction rather than rate of travel.
questions.hint: Remember that a magnitude is a distance, and distances are not signed.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: eliminate a parameter to obtain a Cartesian relation
questions.stem: A curve is given by x of t equal to 2t plus 1 and y of t equal to t squared. Which Cartesian relation results from eliminating the parameter?

options.text: y equals the quantity (x minus 1) squared divided by 4, a parabola opening upward
y equals 4 times the quantity (x minus 1) squared, an inverted squaring of the relation
options.misconception: believes solving for the parameter squares the coefficient in the wrong direction

options.text: x equals 2y plus 1, which treats the roles of the two coordinates as exchanged
options.misconception: believes the simpler-looking coordinate should be solved for the parameter

options.text: y equals x squared, having discarded the constant shift along the x-axis
options.misconception: believes constants vanish when a parameter is eliminated from a pair of equations

questions.explanation: Solving the first equation for the parameter gives t equal to (x minus 1) divided by 2, and substituting that into the second gives y equal to (x minus 1) squared over 4, which is a parabola with vertex at (1, 0). The shift of 1 in the x-coordinate must survive elimination, because it is what places the vertex away from the origin, and dividing rather than multiplying by 2 is the direction the solving actually goes.
questions.hint: Solve the linear coordinate equation for the parameter, then substitute.

options.misconception: believes a Cartesian relation always records the direction of traversal

options.text: It fails to say how fast the point moves, since speed is not a geometric property
options.misconception: believes a Cartesian relation is expected to record a rate of travel

options.text: It fails to say how many times the point passes through the origin on the way round
options.misconception: believes a Cartesian relation should count how often a point is visited

What the relation does keep is the point being on the unit circle; what it drops is the restriction on the parameter and, with it, the part of the curve actually traced.

questions.learningObjective: explain why a polar pair is not unique for a given point

(3, 3π over 4), since adding a quarter turn to the angle reaches the same point

options.text: (−3, π over 4), since a negative radius describes a point on the opposite ray

questions.learningObjective: convert a polar pair to Cartesian coordinates
questions.stem: A point is given in polar form as radius 2 and angle π over 4. What is its x-coordinate in rectangular form? Report the number only.

questions.learningObjective: describe a practical method for plotting a polar curve

options.text: Choose a single convenient angle, draw the radius there, and extend it into a full curve
options.misconception: believes one radius of known length determines the whole shape of the curve

options.text: Convert to Cartesian form by eliminating θ, then sketch using the usual rectangular habits
options.misconception: believes eliminating the parameter preserves which part of the curve is traced

When n is odd the second half of the turn retraces the first half on the opposite side of the origin, so only n distinct petals survive, and when n is even all 2n intervals are distinct and the graph is symmetric about the polar axis.

The radius grows by a constant additive amount for each radian of angle turned
options.misconception: believes the spiral's growth is linear in the angle rather than exponential

options.text: The radius is constant, because a spiral keeps the same distance from the origin

options.misconception: believes the exponential growth factor has a negative exponent in the formula

options.misconception: believes the extra factor arrives as a square root rather than linearly

options.misconception: believes the cosine at angle π is one rather than minus one

questions.explanation: The cosine of π is −1, so the radius is 1 + 2 times −1, which is −1. A negative radius points along the ray opposite to the stated angle, so with the angle at π the point lands on the positive x-axis, and converting gives x = (−1) cos π = 1 and y = (−1) sin π = 0. Dropping the sign would wrongly suggest the radius were 1 and the point still sat on that axis by accident.
questions.hint: Remember that a negative radius reverses the ray, then convert to Cartesian coordinates.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: expose an inverted ratio in a slope or speed computation
questions.stem: A student finds the slope of a parametrised curve by dividing the derivative of x with respect to t by the derivative of y with respect to t. What is wrong with that method?

options.text: The ratio is inverted, because the slope of a curve is the rate of y with respect to x
The ratio is right, but the derivative of x must be taken before the derivative of y
options.misconception: believes the order of taking the two derivatives changes the quotient

options.text: The ratio is meaningless, because two rates of change cannot be divided at a point
options.misconception: believes a quotient of two derivatives is never defined

options.text: The ratio gives the speed rather than the slope, and the speed is what is wanted here
options.misconception: believes a quotient of the two rates measures a rate of travel

questions.explanation: The slope of a curve in the plane is the change in y per unit change in x, so it is the ratio of the two rates with the y rate on top, and the reciprocal the student computes is the slope of the reflected curve instead. Where both rates are nonzero the mistake produces a number close to the reciprocal rather than an obvious nonsense value, which is exactly why it survives. The speed, a separate quantity, is the magnitude of the rate vector and needs no division.
questions.hint: Ask what a unit step in the horizontal direction does to the vertical coordinate.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why vanishing coordinate rates together leave the tangent undetermined
questions.stem: A student claims the curve with x of t equal to t cubed and y of t equal to t squared has a horizontal tangent at t equal to 0. What does the derivative show?

options.text: Both rates vanish there, so the ratio is of the form 0 over 0 and no tangent direction is set
The slope is zero there, because a zero numerator makes the ratio vanish
options.misconception: believes a zero numerator alone settles the slope even when the denominator vanishes too

options.text: The tangent is vertical there, because the derivative of x vanishes at that point
options.misconception: believes a zero x rate means the tangent must be vertical regardless of the y rate

options.text: The claim holds, because a vanishing rate of change of y always means a horizontal tangent
options.misconception: believes a zero y rate alone guarantees a horizontal tangent

questions.explanation: The rates are dx over dt equal to 3t squared and dy over dt equal to 2t, and at t = 0 both are zero, so the quotient of the two is 0 over 0, which fixes nothing. The point is in fact a cusp of the semicubical parabola y cubed equal to x squared, where the tangent does exist but its direction comes from the dominant order of the two rates rather than from their ratio at that instant.
questions.hint: Evaluate both rates at the parameter value before forming any quotient.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: expose an error in which vector a projection factor is applied to
questions.stem: A student projects the vector ⟨1, 4⟩ onto the vector ⟨2, 3⟩ and reports the result as the factor 11 over 13 multiplied by ⟨1, 4⟩ instead of ⟨2, 3⟩. Identify the error.

options.text: The factor was applied to the vector being projected, but it must multiply the target vector
The factor is right, but a projection must also be divided by two to avoid double counting
options.misconception: believes projections require a hidden factor of one half

options.text: The factor is right, but the two vectors must be swapped and the factor recomputed as 17 over 11
options.misconception: believes a projection is symmetric so the roles of the two vectors may be exchanged

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because multiplying either vector by the factor traces the same line
options.misconception: believes the two scaled vectors coincide because they are parallel

questions.explanation: The projection of v onto u is the scale factor times u, so the factor 11 over 13, which is the dot product 11 divided by the squared length 13 of ⟨2, 3⟩, must multiply ⟨2, 3⟩ to give ⟨22 over 13, 33 over 13⟩, not ⟨1, 4⟩. Multiplying ⟨1, 4⟩ by that factor leaves a vector pointing along v rather than along u, so it cannot be the component of v lying along u.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two vectors the factor was built from, and then check the result lies along it.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Centroid of a region under a curve
questions.learningObjective: find the ordinate of a centroid from a region bounded by a curve
questions.stem: A uniform lamina fills the region under the curve y equal to the square root of x, above the x-axis, for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4. What is the y-coordinate of its centroid? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The area is the integral of the root of x from 0 to 4, which is 16 over 3, and the first moment about the x-axis is one half of the integral of the curve squared, which is one half of the integral of x, that is 4. The centroid's height is the moment over the area, so 4 divided by 16 over 3 is 0.75, which sits well below the maximum height of 2 as expected for a region that widens to the right.
questions.hint: Divide the first moment about the x-axis by the total area.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: combine area and moment data for a composite region to find its centroid
questions.stem: A uniform lamina is the union of the rectangle from (0, 0) to (4, 2) and the triangle with base from (0, 2) to (4, 2) and vertex at (2, 5). What is the y-coordinate of its centroid? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The rectangle has area 8 with centroid at height 1, and the triangle has base 4 and height 3, so area 6 with centroid one third of the way up from its base, at height 3. The combined height is therefore (8 times 1 + 6 times 3) over 14, which is 26 over 14, that is 13 over 7, about 1.857. Adding the two areas before adding the moments would discard the weighting that makes this correct.
questions.hint: Weight each piece's height by its own area, then divide by the total area.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the area between a parametrised curve and the x-axis
questions.stem: A curve is traced by x of t equal to t squared and y of t equal to 2t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. What is the area between the curve and the x-axis over that interval? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The area is the integral of the height times the horizontal rate, so it is the integral of 2t times 2t from 0 to 2, that is 4 times the integral of t squared, which is 4 times 8 over 3 and so 32 over 3, about 10.6667. As an independent check, eliminating the parameter gives y equal to 2 times the root of x on 0 to 4, and integrating that directly returns the same 32 over 3.
questions.hint: Set up the height times the horizontal rate and integrate, then cross-check in Cartesian form.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: set up the area integral for a region bounded by a parametrised curve
questions.stem: For the curve traced by x of t equal to t squared and y of t equal to 2t over 0 ≤ t ≤ 2, which integral gives the area between the curve and the x-axis?

options.text: The integral from 0 to 2 of y of t times the derivative of x with respect to t
The integral from 0 to 2 of x of t times the derivative of y with respect to t
options.misconception: believes the height pairs with the vertical rate instead of the horizontal one

options.text: The integral from 0 to 2 of y of t times the derivative of y with respect to t
options.misconception: believes a strip's width is measured by the rate of change of the height

options.text: The integral from 0 to 2 of x of t times the derivative of x with respect to t
options.misconception: believes the strip's height should be the horizontal coordinate itself

questions.explanation: A thin vertical strip has height given by the curve and horizontal width given by the rate of change of x with respect to the parameter, so the area is the integral of the product of those two, which here is the integral of 2t times 2t. Option B and option D pair the coordinates with the wrong rates, and option C measures the width with a vertical rate, so all three describe a different area from the one wanted.
questions.hint: Ask what each thin strip's height and horizontal width are in terms of the parameter.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.learningObjective: expose the overlap that invalidates an application of Pappus's theorem
questions.stem: A student chooses an axis of rotation that passes straight through a proposed planar region, applies Pappus's theorem, and reports a volume. What is the flaw in the reasoning?

options.text: The axis cuts the region, so the swept solid covers some points twice and the product overcounts
The axis must be chosen so that the region is circular, which limits the theorem to discs
options.misconception: believes the theorem applies only when the region happens to be a disc

options.text: The axis must be parallel to the plane of the region, and the student chose a skew line
options.misconception: believes a skew axis is what invalidates the application of the theorem

options.text: The centroid must be found by integration, and the student used a guessed centre instead
options.misconception: believes an approximate centroid is the only thing that can spoil the product

questions.explanation: The theorem multiplies the area by the distance the centroid travels, and it is proved by sweeping the region as a ribbon whose radius is the distance to the axis, so it counts each point of the solid once only when the region lies wholly on one side of the axis. An axis through the interior makes the ribbon wrap over itself, so the product overcounts and the reported volume exceeds the true solid.
questions.hint: Ask whether any part of the swept ribbon passes over the same point twice.
